utterances.text: Well, Mr. Waespi, for some questions which are not directly related to the criminal responsibilities of the accused, I believe that some speculative questioning is allowed, but this piece of the evidence is very sensitive, which is directly related to the alleged criminal activities of the accused. So I'm afraid that this witness is not the proper witness to give some comments and testimony of this piece of the information at this stage. Maybe you could change of your question or maybe in the future you could find some more proper witness to give some evidence on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't want to dispute with you, Mr. President, but we were led to believe that everything was done according to the rules. We have seen allusions to these rules. I just mentioned 74, I believe. And then here we have a witness who basically seems to confirm that. So I believe we are entitled to put it right, to confront him with the way it was really done, not in books but in reality. But if you are saying that this witness can't say anything relevant about the time, he wasn't there, then of course that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I could have a moment, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect, Mr. Stojanovic? Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just one question for Mr. Radovic. I would like to show the witness an exhibit we have used. That's 5 -- 513 -- P513 and P --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the orders, and I would like to ask Mr. Radovic to comment on some points. Re-examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radovic, if you recall, at one point you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please put 124, page 124 in English, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, Mr. Radovic, you said that in the daily order there was an error when it said that days off are to be taken as approved by the company commander and the chief of engineers. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MINJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the order of the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Objection. I don't think that's within the scope of what -- what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I understand your point, but first of all you have to establish the relevance, you know. I believe that the Prosecution used another -- another document, but here we have this document here. You may ask some questions along this line, but first of all there must be some relevance concerning the cross-examination of Mr. Waespi's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I don't think the witness said there was an error. He said he had looked at the wrong document, the way I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: He didn't say there was an error. So if that's your presumption, then it's wrong in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with the Prosecution on this particular issue, but you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that case, I think there is a misunderstanding. We have to -- I have to ask the witness about the 15th of July then, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, would you please look at the daily order of the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to put page 126 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, it says here: "Days off: To be taken only with the approval of the company commander and the chief of engineers."

utterances.speaker: MINJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: If you can look at the daily order for the following day, the 16th of July, does it say anything about days off?

utterances.speaker: MINJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Days off are not to be taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the order on the previous day, the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MINJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: "Days off: To be taken as per the published schedule as approved by the company commander."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it say here that they should also be approved by the chief of engineers?

utterances.speaker: MINJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that on the 15th of July, where it says days off to be taken with the approval of the company commander and chief of engineers, that this is a mistake by the person who typed this up?

utterances.speaker: MINJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't usual for the chief of engineers to approve days off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's again asking for speculation about something. In the event, he wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this case we'll allow the question to be asked and then answered, because it is our intention to know some reasons, and the witness has the right to give some explanations, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic, in the context of the response you gave to Mr. Waespi, did the chief of engineers approve days off for members of the engineers company or was this the task of the company commander?

utterances.speaker: MINJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: It was the task of the company commander, and it was only I who did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Dragan Jokic was in those days in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MINJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: July 1995? I suppose he was in Zvornik. I don't know. I wasn't there, so I can't really know where he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Given the extent of redirect, am I allowed to ask one further question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that all the questions asked by the -- Mr. Stojanovic was within the scope of your cross-examination. I see no reason for you to ask any questions. First of all, in this case we believe that the document speaks for itself. Secondly, the witness was not there. All his answer is kind of speculative nature. With those two understandings, I don't think you should ask any questions again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sure. I wanted to ask him about another speculation, but that's okay, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. D12/3, the summary report in the engineering area. All the other exhibits have already been admitted into evidence, although I'm not sure at this moment whether D12/3 has been admitted. If it has not, I wish to tender it, but I have now been advised that it has already been admitted. Therefore, we have no new exhibits to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I was informed that this document has been already admitted into the evidence, so there's no need for you to tender it once again. On the part of the Prosecution, do you have any documents to tender at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, do you have another witness waiting outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As we agreed, my colleague Mr. Lukic will question the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So there are no protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: By the way, there is a change of schedule. Tomorrow morning we'll sit in this courtroom instead of afternoon since tomorrow is Friday afternoon. And as the rule of rotation, this week we should sit in the afternoon instead of the morning, but since another case is not on, so we moved the cases. Our sitting is in the morning. So tomorrow morning we will resume in the same courtroom at 9.00 instead of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Your direct examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Djuric.

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't have too much time today, so we will try to speed up the examination-in-chief as much as we can. At the same time, I would also like you to pause after I put my question so that the interpreters can have the opportunity to translate everything into English and French. For the record, could you please tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: My name is Brano Djuric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please spell your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: B-r-a-n-o D-j-u-r-i-c diacritic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the two of us met for the first time yesterday evening, there were some errors in your personal data which we provided to the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber, so I would like you to tell us now your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 31st of January, 1960.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: In Mladjevici, municipality of Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which schools did you attend?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I completed the geodesic technical school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completing your schooling, where did you get your first job?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I started to work in the Bosna putevi Sarajevo construction firm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which town did you work?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I worked mostly out in the field because this company does a lot of projects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work in Zvornik before the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live before you came to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Before I came to Zvornik, I lived in Zivinice, and this is where I worked in the municipal geodesic administration, the land surveyors office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that where you were when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you did you leave Zivinice?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I left Zivinice on the 3rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you leave Zivinice?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I left Zivinice because of combat operations. Before that, my wife and children had already left for Banja Koviljaca in the municipality of Loznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how you came to Zvornik. Which route did you take?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I went to Zvornik with an acquaintance of mine, in a car, and we used the Tuzla-Bijeljina-Zvornik route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join - and if so, when - the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I joined the army of Republika Srpska on the 15th of May. I joined the Niksic brigade of the Ilijas municipality. This is my place of origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Ilijas until the end of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after you left Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: I went to the municipality of Zvornik after I left Ilijas. That is where my family found accommodation. After arriving there, I joined the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which unit of the Zvornik Brigade did you become a member of?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of September, 1992, I officially transferred to the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you immediately deployed to one of the platoons of the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Since I was a land surveyor, they believed that a person was needed to record the minefields. So I joined the engineering platoon of the engineering company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you came to the Zvornik Brigade, did you have any rank?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides serving your regular military duty, did you have any other kind of military training?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you trained in mine handling then?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: There were people, soldiers, in the engineering company who were trained in mining and explosive devices, so they came to train the soldiers, the men, to do these tasks, and that is how I was also trained to lay mines and for de-mining. And I also mapped and kept records of the minefields that were laid down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1995, in July, were you still a member of the pioneers platoon of the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us in more detail the structure of the pioneering platoon of the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade in 1995. More specifically, in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: The pioneering -- or the pioneers platoon of the engineering company at the time, in my assessment - I was just a regular soldier at the time - numbered about 15 men who were trained to lay down mines and dismantle them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the pioneers platoon have its commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the pioneers platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: At the time, the commander of the pioneers platoon was Stevo Cvoric. I'm now speaking about July 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there frequent changes in the composition of the pioneers platoon; and, if so, why?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. The pioneers platoon, from the beginning of the war, from 1992 until the end of the war, was re-staffed three times because this is a very dangerous job in wartime, and people were killed either by mines or in combat. Some were killed, some were wounded, so that new men had to be trained three times in order to replenish the pioneers platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the members of the pioneers platoon in one place all the time or were they deployed in different units?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: The members of the pioneers platoon were in one place. Only when the entire line of defence moved, then they operated compactly, as a whole. They would then lay down minefields. In any other case, they were deployed in battalions, in groups of two or three sappers per battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way were orders issued and conveyed to you, the ones that you were supposed to carry out?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Mostly we received oral orders from the company commander. Also, they were conveyed through the means of communication if we were out in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were commands not issued by the platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: In most cases, the platoon commander was also deployed in one of the battalions. In this case, he was deployed together with me to the 3rd Battalion. We called it the Memici battalion. I'm speaking about July 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were deployed in the battalions, did you receive your assignments from the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: We were coordinated by the battalion commander based on their requirements, and we laid down mines in the front section of the line in accordance with how we were trained to do that, with the cooperation of the soldiers of the battalion. This is how we did our job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the form of this cooperation with the soldiers who were assigned to you from the battalion and who were not members of the engineers platoon?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Their primary task was to monitor the enemy to see if we were being watched. They were also supposed to protect us sappers from any possible attacks from the enemy. That was their main assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those soldiers were in fact providing security for you and didn't take part in the mining process itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the pioneers platoon ever received orders from the chief of engineers in the staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Specifically, we didn't receive orders from the chief of engineers but from the commander of the company, or sometimes the platoon commander, if he was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, if you were deployed in the battalions, who did you report to about the tasks you had accomplished?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: While we were mining for the needs of the battalion, we would first report to the battalion commander, submit a report to him, where we worked. Then afterwards, once we arrived back at barracks, we would hand in the records and diagrams of the minefields to the company commander, and then we would deal with all the information in the field, with all the attending diagrams and then compile a final report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report directly to the chief of engineers in the staff and headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: No, never. We never did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your men go to the Wolves of the Drina unit, for example? Were they assigned to them; and, if so, what was their assignment?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: The soldiers of the pioneers platoon were deployed in the platoons of the Vukovi unit only when those units were engaged in battles and combat, and then two soldiers, assault soldiers, were deployed there when they were engaged in offensive operations, and that was their task. If a mine was seen, they had to neutralise that mine, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Faced with a situation when the members of the pioneers platoon were assigned to the Wolves of the Drina, the Drina Wolves unit, were they attached to their commander and resubordinated to their commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Once they were deployed to the Drina Wolves unit, they were subordinated to the platoon commander, the person in charge of the unit engaged in a particular operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you yourself, for example, from the 6th of July up until the 20th of July, 1995? Can you recapitulate and give us your movements during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: From the 6th of July, 1992, I was in the Youth Settlement of Karakaj, which is where the engineers company had its headquarters. I think that sometime around the 10th of July I left together with two other sappers to join the number 3 battalion that was called the Memic Battalion, and I stayed there until the 16th of July, in the evening. 1992 [as interpreted], of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened on the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of July, 1995, what happened was this: The forces of the BH army, and we called them the Muslim forces, from Srebrenica launched - how shall I put this? - a breakthrough towards Tuzla in the region of Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, now we should show the witness the map, and I don't think we have time to go into this area, so if we may make a break at this point and continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. I'm entirely in your hands concerning the break. So we will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. I would like to ask Madam Usher for her help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djuric, when we were talking yesterday, we used a map which was marked by another witness. I would like to ask you to orient yourself on this new map as I put some questions to you on the topic that we will be dealing with now. You said that until the 16th of July, 1995, you were in one place. Can you tell us where you were and also show it on the map.

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of July, 1995, I was in the 3rd Battalion, and that is the axis of Memici, and this is where it is on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That day there was an attack by the 2nd Corps of the army of the B and H, as you said.

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on the 16th after this attack?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: After the attack on the 16th, they informed us in the evening at the battalion command that the engineering platoon should report to Karakaj, and then they brought us to the Youth Settlement, Omladinsko Naselje, in Karakaj, where we spent the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return to the area of Memici over the next few days; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: No. Already the next day, on the 17th of July, a group of sappers - there were about six or seven of us - went to the 4th Battalion in Baljkovica. I'm indicating it here on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which tasks did you receive and who issued these tasks?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: We were tasked by the company commander to go to the 4th Battalion because the line was severed in that area because of the passage of Muslim forces; namely, the VRS pulled back to the left towards Baljkovica and towards this other part. This is where the line was cut. And it was our task to lay mines again in this area in front of the first line of trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This area that you are pointing to, does that have a name, that area or that sector?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: We called this area the Gresnik trench. This is where the line was physically severed for some 2 to 300 metres. It was not possible to lay down trenches there. This Gresnik was at the end of the line, then it was severed, and then on the other side of the river the line of trenches resumed again. The place is actually called Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 17th you left. That is the next day, according to our estimates. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. My group of sappers began to lay mines in front of the lines, because the already existing minefields were quite damaged by the artillery or with the passage of the infantry forces. So we began laying down mines again on the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you complete the laying down of the minefields in that area?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: We stayed there for two more days, I think, the 18th and the 19th, to complete the laying down of the minefield in that sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Dragan Jokic there with you there during that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Major Jokic was there. I saw him on the 18th of July in this Gresnik trench, which I mentioned earlier. That's where I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what happened on the 18th of July, 1995. Do you recall anything of that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Before that - I don't know exactly what time it was, I think it was maybe around noon - we were on a break. I and a couple of my comrades were in a trench. At that moment, the soldiers brought five young boys to the Gresnik trench. They were Muslim boys going towards Tuzla, and that is when our soldiers came upon them quite close to the trench in the grass. They brought them to the trench. I was there at the time. Major Jokic spoke with them, offered to them to eat something for lunch, to drink something. He talked to them, and then at one point he asked, do any of the sappers -- "Are any of the sappers here? We would need to let these boys go, but somebody would need to lead them through the minefields." I was there, so I said, "I'm here, Major, sir." At that point, two other soldiers from the trench went with me to guard me. I walked in front, the two soldiers walked behind me, and then the young boys walked behind them. Of course they were at a distance from me. I was walking ahead because of the mines. At my sign that they should stop, I -- I then continued and I disarmed the mines, and then we would continue to walk. The terrain there is covered with trees. We walked for another 100 metres through these trees. This is not a coloured map so you cannot see where the meadows are and where the woods are. This place here is where the meadows were, and this is where the forest was. I told them to seek shelter behind some trees, and I called out to the Muslim soldiers who were quite close, across from the meadow in their own trenches. At some point one of them responded and asked what we wanted, and then once again I called out loudly, saying that we had some young boys here that I wanted to let through and that they should not shoot and that they should make sure that those boys don't hit any of their mines. They didn't believe us. So I asked the boys to step out into the clearing, into the meadow. Very slowly, a little bit afraid, they did walk out of their cover, and at the moment they saw them they said, "Oh, yes. That is really so." So the three of us, myself and the two soldiers who were guarding me, waited for the other side to take over the boys. It wasn't a large distance. And then we went back to the trench, and as we were going back, I rearmed the mines again. So this is all that I wanted to say about this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question about this: Did you see if the boys made it safely to the other side?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I waited as they were walking across. The grass was quite high, so I waited until they entered into their part of the forest. One of the soldiers from the other side walked ahead to meet them, so I couldn't really see much further. But later, as their soldiers were calling out to each other, I could hear that they had made it safely across to the other side. They also thanked us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that sometime in mid-July there were executions of captured Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't hear about that. I only heard about it when I returned after the 19th or the 20th of July to the engineering company unit. From the stories of other soldiers I heard that something had happened, but I didn't know any details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any official information about those executions?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: No. I was just a regular soldier. I was never informed officially about this by anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you find out about these killings?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: From stories of people, the things that the soldiers were saying and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we will be moving to our last topic that we wish to cover in this examination-in-chief. The period that we will be talking about does not correspond to the period mentioned in the indictment. We will actually be discussing the character of Dragan Jokic. After the signing of the Dayton Accords, did you personally take part in the de-mining in the Zvornik Brigade zone of defence --

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- which were laid down by your pioneers platoon.

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally took place in the de-mining of those minefields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dragan Jokic take part in these operations?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Dragan Jokic took an active part in the de-mining of the terrain, because according to his military occupational speciality, and I forgot to mention this earlier when I was talking about this, sometimes in coordination with us, he also took part in the laying down of minefields so that when the war was ended, he took an active part in the de-mining of those same fields and in the restoration of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us, in which areas did you complete your de-mining, and did some minefields stay uncleared; and if so, why was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade -- actually, the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade worked from the river Spreca in the direction of north-east all the way to the border with the municipality of Ugljevik. But this is much further, you cannot see this on the map. So this is an area about 40 kilometres long, according to my estimates. It's so long because this is not going in a straight line. The sappers de-mined all the mines from the river Spreca via Memici, in this whole area, up until the settlement of Boskovici. In that area the mines were left as they were because there was no record or sketch of the minefields in that area. The mines were too close. The mines were laid down at night. And that area was not officially recorded. So that was the only part that was left over. And then we continued on the other side all the way until the border with the municipality of Ugljevik. That whole area was totally de-mined, and as far as I know, from the time that the war ended up until the present, no single case of any accidents or injuries of civilians by mines were recorded. As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the process of de-mining, did it happen that any of the sappers were wounded and, if so, do you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the area of the village of Setici, Goran Tomic was wounded. That was the name of the sapper. Another one, a new man, was also wounded. His leg was blown off by a mine, so he is an invalid as a result of that accident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war, did the pioneers platoon of the engineers company of the Zvornik Brigade receive any kind of recognition from SFOR for the de-mining that it carried out?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: The SFOR issued oral recognition and commended us for the work that we did. I recall one detail where one high-ranking officer of the US army was showing his soldiers how you could, in a classic and very simple way, keep records and sketches of minefields and then successfully de-mine the same fields without the use of any modern technology. But like I said, these were just oral recognition and commendations that we received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that as to the crimes against the Muslims of Srebrenica, are concerned, you heard that from the stories that were told; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those stories or, rather, the rumours going round, was Dragan Jokic ever mentioned as a perpetrator in those events?

utterances.speaker: BRANO DJURIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, his name was never mentioned in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jokic [sic]. That would be all that the Defence of Mr. Dragan Jokic had to ask you. You will now be answering questions from Mr. Karnavas, if he has any, and from the Prosecution, if they have any, and possibly from Their Honours the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Any questions you put to the witness, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no questions for this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, at this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We used only this map, and it has already been admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there is no document to tender from the Prosecution side. Yes. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for your coming to The Hague to give your testimony. Now the usher will show you out of the room, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, do we have another witness waiting outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. As I promised yesterday, we thought we'd complete these two witnesses today. Our witness for tomorrow will be arriving in the course of the afternoon, and we'll have a talk to him between 6.00 and 8.00, and we'll be ready to go ahead with the examination-in-chief of the next witness tomorrow morning. So we're keeping to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But -- but I think we lose another 50 minutes for today, and since we have a long list of witnesses next week, so if we could do the testimony of the witness as early as possible, that will greatly improve our efficiency. But since we don't have the witness for today, I believe that we have to adjourn, and we will resume tomorrow morning, 9.00, in the same courtroom. The hearing is adjourned.
